analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from corporations that own 50 or more single-family rental homes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on July 10, 2025 and has had no committee vote, hearing, or floor action since, with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The HOMES Act would change the tax code so that any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental homes — counting properties held through affiliates as one owner — could no longer deduct mortgage interest or depreciation on those homes. Those two deductions are a major part of how large landlords lower their tax bills on debt-financed house purchases. The bill carves out affordable housing: owners keep the deductions on low-income tax credit properties and on homes they newly build, and they can deduct interest and depreciation in the year they sell a home to an individual who will live in it or to a nonprofit, land trust, or land bank that preserves affordability. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in neighborhoods where corporate landlords have bought up houses, and first-time buyers who find themselves outbid by all-cash investor offers. The bill raises the after-tax cost of holding large portfolios of single-family rentals, and it gives those owners a tax reason to sell homes to families or to nonprofits and community land trusts. Small landlords with fewer than 50 homes are untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Denies interest and depreciation deductions to any owner of 50 or more single-family rental properties, with properties held through commonly controlled affiliates counted together, raising the after-tax cost of large-scale single-family rental ownership. [S2] [S3]

Lets the owner keep the deductions only in the year a property is sold, and only if it goes to an individual who will occupy it as a home or to a nonprofit, community land trust, land bank, or public housing agency subsidiary — tilting large landlords toward selling to families and affordability organizations. [S2] [S3]
Spares low-income housing tax credit properties and newly constructed rentals, so the penalty does not fall on building new housing. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate owners of single-family rental portfolios, which would lose two deductions worth a substantial share of their returns; to the extent their costs rise, they may attempt to pass some of it to renters through higher rents, and small landlords would keep a tax advantage these owners lose.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises large landlords' costs without directly lowering anyone's rent; if those costs are passed through, some renters in corporate-owned homes could see higher rents rather than relief. [S3]

Owners below the 50-property threshold keep both deductions, so small and mid-sized landlords — and any owner who splits holdings to stay under the line — retain a tax advantage over the large owners the bill targets. [S2] [S3]

The definition of covered property includes buildings of four or fewer units, which reaches some small multifamily buildings, and the statute leans on the Treasury to write rules preventing restructuring to evade the 50-property threshold. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's mechanism is indirect: it does not cap rents or build homes, it changes the tax math for big landlords in the hope that fewer leveraged portfolios means less investor competition for starter homes. The carve-outs for new construction and affordable housing are sensible and narrow the supply risk, but the pass-through concern and the threshold's susceptibility to restructuring are real limits. On balance it targets a concentrated tax advantage that small landlords and ordinary buyers do not get, at modest risk to renters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has not taken it up, so it is sitting in committee while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the HOMES Act on July 10, 2025, joined by Rep. Summer Lee of Pennsylvania, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation. [S1] [S3] [S5]
The bill has one cosponsor and no committee markup, hearing, or floor action in the action history since referral. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No vote has occurred, so the main beneficiaries of the current state of play are large single-family rental owners, who keep the existing interest and depreciation deductions the bill would have taken away, and investors competing for starter homes unchanged. Nothing has been decided yet; the bill could still move, though bills at this stage rarely do.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 10, 2025 and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee. [S1] [S5]

for.name: Rep. Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction. [S3] [S4]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; chair controls the markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill since its July 10, 2025 referral, leaving it without committee action. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been held, so no partisan split is on the record; the bill's sponsor and sole cosponsor are both Democrats, and no Republican has signed on. [S4]

industries.note: These owners would lose interest and depreciation deductions on portfolios of 50 or more houses, directly cutting the after-tax returns that debt-financed single-family rental strategies rely on. Their interest in keeping the current treatment runs against buyers and renters who compete with them for the same homes. [S2] [S3]
They keep the deductions the big owners lose, gaining a relative tax advantage in the rental market. Whether that helps or costs tenants depends on local competition. [S2]

industries.industry: Affordable housing nonprofits, community land trusts, and land banks
industries.note: The bill restores deductions to large owners in the year they sell to these organizations, creating an incentive to move homes into permanently affordable ownership. [S2] [S3]

LIHTC properties are fully exempt from the deduction ban, so the bill leaves the tax-credit affordable housing pipeline untouched and reinforces its role as the favored channel for rental housing investment. [S2] [S3]

analysis.trajectory: A first-year tax bill with a single cosponsor sitting in Ways and Means has very long odds; most tax bills die there unless leadership attaches them to a broader package. Barring a rare push, expect the bill to go unmarked-up for the rest of this Congress.
